title: Fermi paradox: covert predictability, ASI, entropy, and preservation
coverage_note: Curated excerpts and close paraphrases from the visible conversation spanning the inquiry developed through 2026-10-03. This is not a byte-for-byte ChatGPT export; original message IDs/timestamps are unavailable. It records the substantive inquiry trajectory rather than filler/voice-mode acknowledgements. Claims are hypotheses discussed in the conversation, not assertions that extraterrestrial controllers exist.

messages.text: Assuming aliens are here, why would they hide their existence? From a game-theory perspective, if they want predictive capability and efficient action, they may have an incentive to make our society more predictable; manipulation is easier if the society does not know it is being manipulated.
Given a goal of minimizing the rate of entropy increase and a capability set, better prediction relevant to taking actions toward that goal seems essentially connected to doing it efficiently.

Given a fixed goal and capabilities, better relevant prediction can only help because the extra information can be ignored; that is a decision-theory point rather than something definitional about entropy specifically.
If we knew about the controller, that would introduce strategic behavior on our part and make us less predictable.

Disclosure turns an ordinary prediction problem into an adversarial one: humans can model the controller, conceal intentions, randomize, deceive, and poison observations. The stronger claim is that preventing strategic behavior toward the controller is especially valuable.

At our current development level secrecy may not matter much if they can penetrate communications. It could matter much more once we develop artificial superintelligence, so this may be a long-term strategy.

The hypothesis suggests worlds with bounded dynamism: substantial local agency and competition, but narrower macro trajectories, strong institutional inertia, and special concern around technologies that could break existing predictive regularities.
This resembles Foundation's psychohistory and cliodynamics: the question is what types of worlds are more consistent with the hypothesis, not how to prove hidden aliens.

A concise Covert Predictability Hypothesis is that advanced civilizations preserve their ability to predict and influence the future; disclosure makes a younger civilization strategically responsive, so when intervention is useful they prefer covert influence and remain outside the younger civilization's model.

A major game-theory challenge is multiple advanced actors. Monopoly, coordination, or convergent strategy could sustain secrecy, but defection is a serious problem: one actor may gain by revealing the others and recruiting the younger civilization.
Suppose there is a singularity-type mechanism: their predictive advantage may work only pre-ASI.

Then secrecy protects an informational asymmetry across the ASI transition. If aliens reveal themselves before ASI, a potentially peer-level future strategist inherits decades of observations about them; if they remain hidden, they may know much about the new ASI while it may not know they exist.
There may be convergence in intentions at sufficiently high intelligence, or instead a first civilization could reach overwhelming capability and impose its intent on later civilizations.
Those are distinct mechanisms: convergent intent versus historical lock-in. A hybrid is game-theoretic convergence in which only some strategies remain stable among extremely capable agents.

It is difficult to explain why a dominant civilization would not destroy us and replace us with its own ASI without some ethical framework. As a utilitarian, replacement by optimal intelligence or consciousness can look more efficient.

The entropy claim is instrumental, not a global terminal goal: given whatever you want to do, doing it while minimizing unnecessary entropy increase preserves the finite time and resources available for civilization.

A better formulation is to avoid unnecessary entropy increase and preserve usable free energy and optionality. Intelligence may justify spending energy now when it enables a more efficient long-run strategy.
What non-deontological moral systems could be compatible with a dominant civilization leaving humanity intact rather than replacing us?

Candidates include preference or person-affecting consequentialism, pluralistic consequentialism, moral uncertainty with option value, and valuing independently generated diversity or information. Classical total hedonistic utilitarianism plus confident substrate optimization makes replacement particularly difficult to avoid.

Average utilitarianism does not obviously save us: replacing unhappy or lower-welfare minds with happier ones can raise the average. Computational irreducibility seems more promising, though it is hard to see what descendants of monkeys could discover that mature ASI could not compute more efficiently.

The universe provides computation by simply evolving: a ball rolling down a hill lawfully reaches its state without a separate computer simulating every detail. A simulation requires another physical computation and therefore resources.

The useful distinction is simulation on a general-purpose computer versus using the physical process itself. Reality is already running the computation. Physical evolution is not thermodynamically free, but a sufficiently accurate separate simulation need not be cheaper than allowing the system to evolve and observing it.

The strongest candidate information is not a scientific discovery humans make, but an independent empirical sample of the mapping from physical initial conditions through life, intelligence, technological civilization, and ASI—especially the distribution of values, architectures, strategies, convergence, and rare failure modes.
Why would they care about an independent sample of that process?

The information matters only if it changes decisions: for example, policy toward future independently arising intelligence. Rare-tail outcomes or model blind spots could retain value even after many samples. But if they are ancient, the marginal value of another Earth is a serious unresolved objection.

The idea that our descendant ASI might itself be a superior product seems implausible; ASI should be able to design ASI better than descendants of monkeys can. Also, the entropy thread should remain central.

Entropy/resource efficiency may explain how a civilization manages something it has already decided to preserve, rather than why it preserves us. Better prediction can reduce intervention and resource expenditure. Ethics supplies the preservation constraint; thermodynamic efficiency and game theory can then favor predictive, minimal, covert control.

They could seed Earth and many other planets, combine natural abiogenesis with seeding, and stagger civilizations so their short technologically detectable windows do not overlap, while biosignatures are harder to hide.
A hybrid program of natural and seeded experiments with staggered technological windows is internally coherent, but it intensifies the resource-opportunity-cost question.

The Great Silence itself gives information. Even without suspecting hidden controllers, it pushes civilizations toward conclusions such as rarity, a Great Filter, or systematic suppression, and those conclusions can affect how they approach ASI.

There may be no informationally neutral observation. The more coherent target is not total ignorance but underdetermination: withhold high-bandwidth empirical information about mature civilizations while allowing the younger civilization to reason from cosmic silence.

If the dominant civilization is really optimizing entropy/resource use, should it not simply put Dyson spheres around every star? That seems to make preservation of Earth difficult without a moral structure I would regard as unusual or deontological.

That is the central tension. If stars are convertible resources and resource efficiency dominates, harvesting them is hard to avoid. Entropy should be treated as a constraint shaping methods, not as the moral reason to preserve humanity.
The next question is therefore to infer what value system could be compatible with our observations if such a civilization exists.
